newsitem.title: MEXICO: INSTANT VIEW-Analysts shrug off Mexico trade data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Analysts shrug off Mexico trade data.

text.p: A drop in April's trade surplus to $50 million from a preliminary $109 million suggests Mexico could move into a trade deficit sooner than expected, but most economists said on Wednesday they were cheered by signs the domestic market is strengthening.
RAUL RAMIREZ, VICE-PRESIDENT, BANQUE NATIONALE DE PARIS
"It's bad news for export growth, but it is good news for the internal market. These goods are being consumed by someone," he said.

"We were surprised by the preliminary figure, but we think today's number is normal. We're not nervous or concerned," he added. "Some locals will be spooked by this, but capital market investors are willing to finance Mexico... and in the money markets, Mexico won't suffer a lot."
He said the April figure meant Mexico's trade surplus could turn into a deficit sooner than expected.
"It could be next month, in May. For sure after the summer, with the influx of goods ahead of Christmas, we will have a small deficit," he said.
"Some people are obviously going to say we're deteriorating on the trade side, but this is on balance positive."
"Manufacturing exports have been accelerating in the past few months...and the fact that there is a surge in consumer imports also has to be a positive."

"People are far more worried right now about the pace of economic recovery than they are about deterioration in the trade balance. And after the capital account numbers, it looks as if the balance of payments situation is still positive for the peso," he said.
Asked whether the peso would take a hit, he said: "Not much of one, if any."
DENIS PARISIEN, VICE PRESIDENT, BANKERS TRUST, NEW YORK
"The move towards a trade deficit seems to be coming a bit earlier than expected."

"(The sharp rise in imports) suggests that the long-awaited growth in private consumption may be arriving at last, but it could also be a due to rebuilding of inventories after several months of low import growth, in anticipation of improved conditions in the third and fourth quarter," he said.
"Surveys show the market was expecting a revision upwards, so this should raise some eyebrows," he added.

"In seasonally adjusted terms, this is quite into negative territory. In seasonally adjusted terms, this is the first time it's been in deficit since January 1995." ((-- Caroline Brothers, Mexico City newsroom +525 728 7905))
